newsitem.title: ABU DHABI: Britain, UAE sign defence pact - official.
newsitem.headline: Britain, UAE sign defence pact - official.

text.p: Britain and the United Arab Emirates on Thursday signed a defence cooperation pact pledging British help if the Gulf state is threatened, officials said.
The agreement was signed by visiting British Defence Secretary Michael Portillo and Sheikh Hamdan bin Zaid al-Nahayan, UAE Minister of State for Foreign Affairs.

The defence accord provides for strengthening military cooperation between Britain and the UAE in such fields as training, combined exercises, provision of modern defence equipment and related services to the UAE armed forces, the development of joint military plans and deployment strategies for the defence of the UAE.
Portillo told Reuters in an interview: "What the agreement commits us to now is working out joint plans and we would like to get on with that beginning in the next few days."

Portillo could not say whether any specific defence contracts would flow from the agreement, but he said the UAE had an active defence procurement policy and there might be opportunities for cooperation with Britain in that.
Portillo earlier held talks with Sheikh Hamdan and his brother Sheikh Mohammed bin Zaid, who is chief of staff of the UAE armed forces.
The UAE, sparsely populated but enriched with huge oil wealth, is nervous about an arms buildup by non-Arab Iran, the largest power in the volatile Gulf region.
The defence accord had been delayed by disagreement over whose laws would apply to British troops operating in UAE territory.
Britain said armed forces traditionally were responsible to their own government, even when operating in another country.
The UAE insisted any British troops deployed in its territory must be liable to its jurisdiction.

The UAE, which celebrates its silver jubilee on Monday, was formed in 1971 when Britain unilaterally withdrew its protection from the Gulf's Trucial States, which it had defended and ruled for 150 years.
The country is now one of the world's richest thanks to abundant supplies of oil and sufficient reserves to last a century.
Its defence pacts with the United States and France have helped lead to military contracts worth more than $4.3 billion in the last three years.
